common_name: Lord Camden Daylily (Crimson-Raspberry Annie T. Giles Award Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Lord Camden holds its small, bright crimson-raspberry blooms well through midseason heat and increases into dense, floriferous clumps.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Lord Camden, registered by hybridizer Kennedy in 1974, bears a bright crimson-raspberry self flower about four and a quarter inches wide with a green throat on a compact 24-inch dormant plant, and it won the American Hemerocallis Society's Annie T. Giles Award for best small-flowered daylily in 1981. Its saturated, nearly red color held up unusually well for its era, which kept it in wide cultivation decades after introduction. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Sugar Cookie Daylily (Fragrant Ivory Annie T. Giles Award Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Sugar Cookie is a compact evergreen daylily valued for its fragrance and clean, circular ivory blooms.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Sugar Cookie, hybridized by Apps and introduced in 1983, bears circular, cream-to-ivory self flowers about three and a quarter inches across with recurved tepals and a green throat, carried on compact 21-inch evergreen scapes, and it won the American Hemerocallis Society's Annie T. Giles Award for best small-flowered daylily in 1989. It is notably fragrant for a small-flowered cultivar and blooms in early-to-midseason with a long flowering window. Divide every three to four years in spring to keep clumps vigorous.

common_name: Siloam Merle Kent Daylily (Orchid-Pink Eyed Double-Award Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Siloam Merle Kent bears small, boldly eyed orchid-pink blooms and is one of the most decorated cultivars in the Siloam series.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Siloam Merle Kent, bred by Pauline Henry and registered in 1984, bears small, bright orchid-pink trumpet blooms about three and a half inches wide with a contrasting deep purple eyezone, pie-crust petal edges, and a green throat. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Annie T. Giles Award for best small-flowered daylily in 1992 and the Don C. Stevens Award for best eyed or banded daylily in 1999, a rare double honor that reflects how cleanly its eye pattern reads on a small flower. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain bloom count.

common_name: Pumpkin Kid Daylily (Orange Eyed Don C. Stevens Award Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Pumpkin Kid is a vigorous reblooming eyed daylily with extended-hour blooms.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Pumpkin Kid, hybridized by Spalding and registered in 1987, bears light-orange flowers about five and a half inches wide with a bold red eyezone and green throat, carried on 18-inch evergreen scapes with extended bloom hours and rebloom. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Don C. Stevens Award for best eyed or banded daylily in 1992, and its large eye-to-petal contrast made it an influential eyed-pattern breeder for subsequent decades. Divide every three to four years in spring to keep the clump floriferous.

common_name: Paige's Pinata Daylily (Peach and Pink Eyed Don C. Stevens Award Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Paige's Pinata is a semi-evergreen eyed daylily with a long extended-hour bloom season.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Paige's Pinata, introduced by Dan Hansen in 1990, bears peach flowers about six inches wide with a rich pink eyezone and yellow throat, the creped petals holding slightly ruffled edges on 26-inch semi-evergreen scapes with extended bloom hours and rebloom. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Don C. Stevens Award for best eyed or banded daylily in 1998. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous flowering.

common_name: A Little Twisted Daylily (Yellow-Green Crispate-Cascade Unusual Form Spider Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; A Little Twisted is a tall, heavily budded unusual-form spider daylily that reblooms through the season.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. A Little Twisted, registered by Scott Elliott in 2015, is an Unusual Form (UF) spider daylily with a petal length-to-width ratio over 5:1, displaying a crispate-cascade twist in bright yellow-green petals banded with a dark red chevron pattern and yellow midribs above an extended green throat, on semi-evergreen 38-inch scapes that bloom early and rebloom. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Harris Olson Spider Award for best spider daylily in 2024 after also taking numerous regional Best Spider and Best-in-Show honors. Divide every three to four years in spring to maintain bud count.

common_name: Tender Love Daylily (Fragrant Flesh-Pink L. Ernest Plouf Award Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Tender Love is a very late, heavily fragrant dormant daylily best suited to gardens with a sustained winter chill.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Tender Love, hybridized by Yancey-Harrison and registered in 1970, bears large, six-and-a-half-inch creamy flesh-pink blooms with a soft yellow halo and green throat, their petals showing subtle rippling ruffles, on dormant scapes that bloom very late in the season. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's L. Ernest Plouf Award for best fragrant daylily in 1980, a now-discontinued award that ran from 1979 to 2003, and remains one of the most strongly scented cultivars from its era. Divide every three to four years in spring to keep clumps floriferous.

common_name: Orange Velvet Daylily (Lenington All-American Award Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Orange Velvet is a vigorous reblooming daylily noted for wide geographic garden performance.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Orange Velvet, hybridized by Joiner in 1988 from a cross of Copper Lantern and Golden Scroll, bears six-and-a-half-inch orange self flowers with a green throat and a diamond-dusted, velvety sheen on heavy-substance petals, carried on strong, upright 30-inch semi-evergreen scapes that bloom midseason and rebloom. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Lenington All-American Award in 1999, an honor given to the cultivar judged the best performer across a wide range of climates and regions. Divide every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Paper Butterfly Daylily (Peach Eyed Lenington All-American Award Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Paper Butterfly is a widely adaptable eyed daylily that blooms early and reblooms over a long season.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Paper Butterfly, hybridized by Morss and registered in 1983, bears six-inch pale-peach flowers with a blue-violet to purple eyezone and yellow throat, blooming early in the season with strong rebloom. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Don C. Stevens Award for best eyed or banded daylily in 1987 and the Lenington All-American Award for wide regional garden performance in 1998, a rare pairing that reflects both its crisp eye pattern and its reliability across climates. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain bloom.

common_name: Kate Carpenter Daylily (Fragrant Creamy Pink Lenington All-American Award Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Kate Carpenter is a widely adaptable evergreen tetraploid daylily praised for consistent garden performance.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Kate Carpenter, hybridized by R.W. Munson in 1980, bears round, flat, ruffled six-inch creamy melon-to-pink self flowers with wavy edges, yellow accents, and a green throat on evergreen, fragrant, 28-inch tetraploid scapes that bloom in early midseason and rebloom. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Lenington All-American Award in 1996, recognizing its reliable performance across a wide range of growing regions. Divide every three to four years in spring to keep clumps vigorous and floriferous.

common_name: Designer Jeans Daylily (Lavender Eyed Lenington All-American Award Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Designer Jeans is a widely adaptable dormant tetraploid daylily valued for dependable garden performance.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Designer Jeans, hybridized by Sara Sikes and registered in 1983, bears six-and-a-half-inch lavender flowers with a darker lavender edge, a lavender eyezone, and a yellow-green throat, carried on dormant, tetraploid, 34-inch scapes that bloom midseason. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Lenington All-American Award in 1995, an award given for the best performance across a wide range of regions and climates. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Plum Cupcake Daylily (Fragrant Miniature Double Donn Fischer Memorial Cup Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Plum Cupcake is a compact, heavily budded miniature double daylily with a long rebloom season.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Plum Cupcake, hybridized by Tim Herrington and registered in 1998, is a fully double miniature daylily with ivory-cream petals, a plum-colored eyezone, and a green throat on a compact, semi-evergreen, fragrant 24-inch plant bearing roughly twenty-five buds across seven branches, blooming early-midseason with rebloom. It received the American Hemerocallis Society's Donn Fischer Memorial Cup for best miniature-flowered daylily, awarded to registered cultivars with blooms under three inches across. Divide every three to four years in spring to keep clumps compact and floriferous.

common_name: Double My Sunshine Daylily (Fragrant Chartreuse Double Ida Munson Award Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Double My Sunshine is a tall, heavily double, strongly fragrant tetraploid daylily.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Double My Sunshine, hybridized by Dianna Gossard and registered in 2012, bears a large, nearly nine-inch, solid chartreuse-yellow-green hose-in-hose double flower that is strongly fragrant, carried on tetraploid, 36-inch scapes that bloom midseason and rebloom. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Ida Munson Award for best double-flowered daylily in 2025. Its double form holds reliably even in heat, and divisions should be split every three to four years in spring to keep clumps vigorous.

common_name: Mayor of Cornatzer Daylily (Yellow Peony-Form Ida Munson Award Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Mayor of Cornatzer is a tall, heavily double daylily with peony-style blooms and strong rebloom.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Mayor of Cornatzer, hybridized by Scott Elliott from a cross of Arms Reaching Out and Beware the Wizard and registered in 2016, bears bright yellow, peony-style double flowers about six inches wide with an orange eye, opening at essentially 100 percent double form on dormant, diploid, 39-inch scapes that bloom midseason and rebloom. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Ida Munson Award for best double-flowered daylily in 2023 after earlier Honorable Mention and Award of Merit honors. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain its full double form.
